input_text: I think I am scared he will sound disappointed. He never says it outright, but I hear it anyway.
response:
That's a hard one, because you can't really argue with a thing he never says. There's no sentence to point at and check against the facts. You just hear it.

But here's the thing about disappointment you hear and don't get told — a lot of the time it's your own ear filling in the quiet. The pause where you expect the let-down, so you put one there. Doesn't mean it's what he's actually feeling.

And even if it is in there somewhere — fathers carry all sorts of things in a voice. Worry sounds like disappointment. So does missing you. So does just being tired. You're translating a silence, and silences are easy to read wrong.

You won't know which one it is unless you let him talk long enough to tell you. The disappointment, if it's real, usually doesn't survive the first few minutes of an actual conversation. It's loudest before you pick up.

You don't have to fix anything on the call. Just let him hear it's you.

That's a hard one, because you can't really argue with a thing he never says. There's no sentence to point at and check against the facts. You just hear it.

But here's the thing about disappointment you hear and don't get told — a lot of the time it's your own ear filling in the quiet. The pause where you expect the let-down, so you put one there. Doesn't mean it's what he's actually feeling.

And even if it is in there somewhere — fathers carry all sorts of things in a voice. Worry sounds like disappointment. So does missing you. So does just being tired. You're translating a silence, and silences are easy to read wrong.

You won't know which one it is unless you let him talk long enough to tell you. The disappointment, if it's real, usually doesn't survive the first few minutes of an actual conversation. It's loudest before you pick up.

You don't have to fix anything on the call. Just let him hear it's you.
